raw_evidence.label: Visual Capitalist's ER-by-state map and its takeaway
raw_evidence.content: TidyTuesday curators frame the week around a Visual Capitalist infographic by Kayla Zhu and Christina Kostandi titled 'Mapped: Emergency Room Visit Times by State.' The map color-codes states from 1h50m for North Dakota up to 5h14m for the District of Columbia, with Puerto Rico second-longest at 4h41m and South Dakota and Nebraska tied with North Dakota for the fastest tier. The article's core observation is that wait times do not track linearly with state population — the densest jurisdictions are slow, but several mid-size states sit near the bottom of the rankings — pointing readers toward staffing, hospital capacity, and uninsured rates as moderating variables. This framing is the natural starting point for our blog because the dataset reproduces exactly the OP-18b values the infographic is built on.

sources.title: Mapped: Emergency Room Visit Times by State | Visual Capitalist
facts: Washington DC averaged 5 hours 14 minutes, the longest in the United States
North Dakota averaged 1 hour 50 minutes, the shortest in the country
Puerto Rico was second-longest at 4 hours 41 minutes
South Dakota at 1h53m and Nebraska at 1h54m rounded out the three fastest

raw_evidence.label: ED boarding crisis: the upstream cause behind long waits
raw_evidence.content: Long ED times are not a triage problem; they are a hospital-capacity problem. ACEP and AHRQ describe the United States as being in a multi-year emergency department 'boarding crisis,' where admitted patients are held in the ED — sometimes for days — because no inpatient bed is available. A 2024 ACEP poll of 2,164 U.S. adults found that 44% of respondents said they or a loved one had experienced long waits in emergency departments, with 16% waiting 13 or more hours before being admitted or transferred. A study released in October 2024 found that boarding admitted patients in the ED nearly doubles the daily cost of their care, while EMRA's April 2024 review documents how boarding produces ambulance diversion, missed treatments, increased mortality, and clinician burnout. This explains why metrics like OP-18b have remained stubbornly elevated even as patient volumes have stabilized post-pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: OP-18b: median ED time as the headline metric
raw_evidence.content: The most-cited measure in this dataset is OP-18b, the median number of minutes patients spend in the emergency department from arrival to leaving the visit (excluding admitted, transferred, or psychiatric patients). CMS treats lower values as better. National median ED time was about 161 minutes in 2024, down marginally from 163 in 2023 — a level the American College of Emergency Physicians describes as a public health crisis. OP-18b is paired with two sibling measures in this dataset: OP-18b_HIGH_MIN (the longer time for patients who were eventually sent home) and OP-18b_LOW_MIN (the shorter time for the lowest-acuity patients), giving a profile of how long the slowest and fastest patients wait at any state's hospitals on average.

raw_evidence.label: Top 10 longest ED waits — DC and PR tower over the rest
raw_evidence.content: The longest median ED times all sit on the Eastern seaboard or in the territories. DC leads at 310 minutes, with Puerto Rico close behind at 302. After a 50-minute gap, Maryland (251), Rhode Island (224), and Delaware (217) form a second tier. Massachusetts (216), New York (199), Connecticut (193), North Carolina (192), and New Jersey (187) round out the top 10. Nine of the top 10 are in the Northeast / Mid-Atlantic corridor — the densest, most insurance-volatile, and most boarding-affected region of the country.

op18b_sorted['rank'] = op18b_sorted.index + 1
print(op18b_sorted[['rank', 'state', 'score']].head(10).to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: ED boarding crisis: the upstream cause behind long waits
raw_evidence.content: Long ED times are not a triage problem; they are a hospital-capacity problem. ACEP and AHRQ describe the United States as being in a multi-year emergency department 'boarding crisis,' where admitted patients are held in the ED — sometimes for days — because no inpatient bed is available. A 2024 ACEP poll of 2,164 U.S. adults found that 44% of respondents said they or a loved one had experienced long waits in emergency departments, with 16% waiting 13 or more hours before being admitted or transferred. A study released in October 2024 found that boarding admitted patients in the ED nearly doubles the daily cost of their care, while EMRA's April 2024 review documents how boarding produces ambulance diversion, missed treatments, increased mortality, and clinician burnout. This explains why metrics like OP-18b have remained stubbornly elevated even as patient volumes have stabilized post-pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: OP-18b: median ED time as the headline metric
raw_evidence.content: The most-cited measure in this dataset is OP-18b, the median number of minutes patients spend in the emergency department from arrival to leaving the visit (excluding admitted, transferred, or psychiatric patients). CMS treats lower values as better. National median ED time was about 161 minutes in 2024, down marginally from 163 in 2023 — a level the American College of Emergency Physicians describes as a public health crisis. OP-18b is paired with two sibling measures in this dataset: OP-18b_HIGH_MIN (the longer time for patients who were eventually sent home) and OP-18b_LOW_MIN (the shorter time for the lowest-acuity patients), giving a profile of how long the slowest and fastest patients wait at any state's hospitals on average.

raw_evidence.label: Visual Capitalist's ER-by-state map and its takeaway
raw_evidence.content: TidyTuesday curators frame the week around a Visual Capitalist infographic by Kayla Zhu and Christina Kostandi titled 'Mapped: Emergency Room Visit Times by State.' The map color-codes states from 1h50m for North Dakota up to 5h14m for the District of Columbia, with Puerto Rico second-longest at 4h41m and South Dakota and Nebraska tied with North Dakota for the fastest tier. The article's core observation is that wait times do not track linearly with state population — the densest jurisdictions are slow, but several mid-size states sit near the bottom of the rankings — pointing readers toward staffing, hospital capacity, and uninsured rates as moderating variables. This framing is the natural starting point for our blog because the dataset reproduces exactly the OP-18b values the infographic is built on.

raw_evidence.label: ED boarding crisis: the upstream cause behind long waits
raw_evidence.content: Long ED times are not a triage problem; they are a hospital-capacity problem. ACEP and AHRQ describe the United States as being in a multi-year emergency department 'boarding crisis,' where admitted patients are held in the ED — sometimes for days — because no inpatient bed is available. A 2024 ACEP poll of 2,164 U.S. adults found that 44% of respondents said they or a loved one had experienced long waits in emergency departments, with 16% waiting 13 or more hours before being admitted or transferred. A study released in October 2024 found that boarding admitted patients in the ED nearly doubles the daily cost of their care, while EMRA's April 2024 review documents how boarding produces ambulance diversion, missed treatments, increased mortality, and clinician burnout. This explains why metrics like OP-18b have remained stubbornly elevated even as patient volumes have stabilized post-pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: OP-18b: median ED time as the headline metric
raw_evidence.content: The most-cited measure in this dataset is OP-18b, the median number of minutes patients spend in the emergency department from arrival to leaving the visit (excluding admitted, transferred, or psychiatric patients). CMS treats lower values as better. National median ED time was about 161 minutes in 2024, down marginally from 163 in 2023 — a level the American College of Emergency Physicians describes as a public health crisis. OP-18b is paired with two sibling measures in this dataset: OP-18b_HIGH_MIN (the longer time for patients who were eventually sent home) and OP-18b_LOW_MIN (the shorter time for the lowest-acuity patients), giving a profile of how long the slowest and fastest patients wait at any state's hospitals on average.

raw_evidence.label: Why population alone does not predict ED time
raw_evidence.content: The Visual Capitalist piece explicitly raises the question that TidyTuesday's prompt repeats: is there a connection between state population and wait times? The answer in the literature is 'partly, but it is dominated by hospital-side variables.' A 2015 PMC paper on risk-adjusted variation in ED timeliness measures found that case mix, hospital size, urban-rural status, and inpatient occupancy explained more variance in OP-18b than population density did. This means we should expect population to be correlated but not deterministic — a useful frame for our scatter plots, where outliers (low-population territories like DC and PR with very high waits, or large states like Texas with mid-pack waits) are the most informative cases.

raw_evidence.label: Acuity gradient: high-volume EDs add ~66 min over low-volume
raw_evidence.content: OP_18b is reported by ED volume tier (Low / Medium / High / Very High). National medians climb monotonically: Low-volume EDs report 126 minutes, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 — a 66-minute jump from the smallest to the busiest sites. State-level gaps inside this same data are often dramatic: New Mexico's Very-High-volume EDs run 164 minutes longer than its Low-volume EDs (134 -> 298 min). Indiana is the outlier in the other direction (-5 min — its busiest EDs are slightly faster than its smallest). The size of the within-state acuity gap is itself a hospital-system-design signal, separate from a state's headline OP_18b.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Acuity gradient (low/medium/high/very_high) by state ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
acu_ids = ['OP_18b_LOW_MIN', 'OP_18b_MEDIUM_MIN', 'OP_18b_HIGH_MIN', 'OP_18b_VERY_HIGH_MIN']
acu = df[df.measure_id.isin(acu_ids)].dropna(subset=['score']).copy()
acu_pivot = acu.pivot(index='state', columns='measure_id', values='score')
acu_pivot = acu_pivot[acu_ids]
acu_pivot.columns = ['Low', 'Medium', 'High', 'Very High']
acu_pivot['range'] = acu_pivot['Very High'] - acu_pivot['Low']
print("national medians by acuity:")
for col in ['Low', 'Medium', 'High', 'Very High']:
    print(f"  {col}: {acu_pivot[col].median():.0f} min")
print(f"\nstate with biggest acuity gap (Very High - Low): {acu_pivot['range'].idxmax()} ({acu_pivot['range'].max():.0f} min)")
print(f"state with smallest gap: {acu_pivot['range'].idxmin()} ({acu_pivot['range'].min():.0f} min)")
print("\nfull table (first 15 by Very High):")
print(acu_pivot.sort_values('Very High', ascending=False).head(15).round(0).to_string())
raw_evidence.output: national medians: Low 126, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 min. NM range 164 min; IN range -5 min.

raw_evidence.label: Acuity gradient: high-volume EDs add ~66 min over low-volume
raw_evidence.content: OP_18b is reported by ED volume tier (Low / Medium / High / Very High). National medians climb monotonically: Low-volume EDs report 126 minutes, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 — a 66-minute jump from the smallest to the busiest sites. State-level gaps inside this same data are often dramatic: New Mexico's Very-High-volume EDs run 164 minutes longer than its Low-volume EDs (134 -> 298 min). Indiana is the outlier in the other direction (-5 min — its busiest EDs are slightly faster than its smallest). The size of the within-state acuity gap is itself a hospital-system-design signal, separate from a state's headline OP_18b.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Acuity gradient (low/medium/high/very_high) by state ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
acu_ids = ['OP_18b_LOW_MIN', 'OP_18b_MEDIUM_MIN', 'OP_18b_HIGH_MIN', 'OP_18b_VERY_HIGH_MIN']
acu = df[df.measure_id.isin(acu_ids)].dropna(subset=['score']).copy()
acu_pivot = acu.pivot(index='state', columns='measure_id', values='score')
acu_pivot = acu_pivot[acu_ids]
acu_pivot.columns = ['Low', 'Medium', 'High', 'Very High']
acu_pivot['range'] = acu_pivot['Very High'] - acu_pivot['Low']
print("national medians by acuity:")
for col in ['Low', 'Medium', 'High', 'Very High']:
    print(f"  {col}: {acu_pivot[col].median():.0f} min")
print(f"\nstate with biggest acuity gap (Very High - Low): {acu_pivot['range'].idxmax()} ({acu_pivot['range'].max():.0f} min)")
print(f"state with smallest gap: {acu_pivot['range'].idxmin()} ({acu_pivot['range'].min():.0f} min)")
print("\nfull table (first 15 by Very High):")
print(acu_pivot.sort_values('Very High', ascending=False).head(15).round(0).to_string())
raw_evidence.output: national medians: Low 126, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 min. NM range 164 min; IN range -5 min.

raw_evidence.content: Long ED times are not a triage problem; they are a hospital-capacity problem. ACEP and AHRQ describe the United States as being in a multi-year emergency department 'boarding crisis,' where admitted patients are held in the ED — sometimes for days — because no inpatient bed is available. raw_evidence.label: Healthcare worker COVID-19 vaccination has collapsed
raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains a non-ED measure that is just as striking as ED waits: HCP_COVID_19, the share of a hospital's healthcare personnel who are 'up to date' with COVID-19 vaccinations. CDC reporting shows that, for the 2023-24 respiratory season, only 15.3% of acute-care hospital personnel and 10.5% of nursing-home personnel were up to date — far below the 76.3% who got an influenza shot in the same period. National coverage rose modestly to 40.2% across all healthcare worker categories for the 2024-25 season, but state-level variation remains enormous, and the values in the TidyTuesday file (which reflect Q1 2024 reporting) sit at the floor of that distribution. The flu measure (IMM_3) in the dataset is a useful within-hospital benchmark: same workforce, same workplace policies, completely different uptake.

raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains a non-ED measure that is just as striking as ED waits: HCP_COVID_19, the share of a hospital's healthcare personnel who are 'up to date' with COVID-19 vaccinations. CDC reporting shows that, for the 2023-24 respiratory season, only 15.3% of acute-care hospital personnel and 10.5% of nursing-home personnel were up to date — far below the 76.3% who got an influenza shot in the same period. National coverage rose modestly to 40.2% across all healthcare worker categories for the 2024-25 season, but state-level variation remains enormous, and the values in the TidyTuesday file (which reflect Q1 2024 reporting) sit at the floor of that distribution. The flu measure (IMM_3) in the dataset is a useful within-hospital benchmark: same workforce, same workplace policies, completely different uptake.

raw_evidence.label: Same workforce, same workplaces — 65.6 pp flu/COVID gap
raw_evidence.content: Inside the very same hospitals, the same employees who get flu shots overwhelmingly do not stay current on COVID boosters. The mean state-level gap (flu pct - COVID pct) is 65.6 percentage points. The smallest gap is Puerto Rico at -3 pp (covid actually higher than flu — a complete inversion). The widest gap is DC at 87.4 pp (94% flu, 6.6% COVID). Twelve states have gaps above 80 pp. This is a within-hospital signal: the same processes that achieve >80% flu coverage are not being applied to COVID, indicating a policy and motivation gap rather than an access gap.

# --- ana_16: COVID vs flu side by side, all states ---
print("\n=== ana_16 ===")
m = covid.set_index('state')['score'].rename('covid').to_frame().join(
    flu.set_index('state')['score'].rename('flu'), how='inner')
m['gap'] = m['flu'] - m['covid']
print(f"national medians: covid {m.covid.median():.1f}%, flu {m.flu.median():.1f}%")
print(f"average gap (flu - covid): {m.gap.mean():.1f} percentage points")
print(f"smallest gap: {m.gap.idxmin()} ({m.gap.min():.1f} pp)")
print(f"largest gap: {m.gap.idxmax()} ({m.gap.max():.1f} pp)")
print('full table sorted by gap:')
print(m.sort_values('gap', ascending=False).round(1).to_string())

raw_evidence.content: Beyond the ED-flow and vaccination measures, the file carries condition-specific 'process bundles.' The contrast — sepsis is hard to keep above 60% even today, stroke care has been pushed near ceiling — is itself one of the most teachable findings the data offers a general reader.

raw_evidence.label: Higher COVID coverage tracks longer ED times (r=0.44)
raw_evidence.content: Counterintuitively, jurisdictions with higher HCP_COVID_19 coverage tend to have longer ED times. Pearson r = 0.44 (Spearman 0.25) across the 52 jurisdictions. This does NOT imply boosters slow down EDs — both are downstream of population density, hospital occupancy, and policy environment: the urban, blue-state, mandate-friendly jurisdictions (MA, NJ, IL) sit toward the top on both axes, while rural Plains states (ND, SD, NE) sit toward the bottom on both. PR is the standout outlier: 62% covid + 302-min ED, far above the trend line in both directions.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_17: COVID coverage vs ED time correlation ---
print("\n=== ana_17 ===")
op18b = df[df.measure_id == 'OP_18b'].dropna(subset=['score'])
covid_ed = covid.set_index('state')['score'].rename('covid_pct').to_frame().join(
    op18b.set_index('state')['score'].rename('ed_min'), how='inner')
corr = covid_ed['covid_pct'].corr(covid_ed['ed_min'])
print(f"Pearson corr (covid up-to-date vs ED median): r = {corr:.3f} (n={len(covid_ed)})")
# Spearman for monotone
sp = covid_ed['covid_pct'].corr(covid_ed['ed_min'], method='spearman')
print(f"Spearman: rho = {sp:.3f}")
print(covid_ed.sort_values('ed_min', ascending=False).round(1).to_string())
raw_evidence.output: Pearson r = 0.441 (n=52); Spearman rho = 0.248

raw_evidence.label: Higher COVID coverage tracks longer ED times (r=0.44)
raw_evidence.content: Counterintuitively, jurisdictions with higher HCP_COVID_19 coverage tend to have longer ED times. Pearson r = 0.44 (Spearman 0.25) across the 52 jurisdictions. This does NOT imply boosters slow down EDs — both are downstream of population density, hospital occupancy, and policy environment: the urban, blue-state, mandate-friendly jurisdictions (MA, NJ, IL) sit toward the top on both axes, while rural Plains states (ND, SD, NE) sit toward the bottom on both. PR is the standout outlier: 62% covid + 302-min ED, far above the trend line in both directions.

    op18b.set_index('state')['score'].rename('ed_min'), how='inner')

Source: Timely and Effective Care - State | Provider Data Catalog (data dictionary) (https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/dataset/apyc-v239) Facts: Footnote 5: results are not available for this reporting period; Footnote 25: state and national averages include VHA hospital data | det_10: Scope guidance for the Analyst.

raw_evidence.label: Reading footnotes 5, 25, and 26
raw_evidence.content: The dataset has three relevant footnotes. Footnote 5 means 'Results are not available for this reporting period' — i.e., the score field is missing because the state did not report or did not have enough cases. Footnotes 25 and 26 mean the reported state and national averages include Veterans Health Administration and Department of Defense hospitals, respectively. These distinctions matter because territories (Guam, AS, MP, VI) frequently carry footnote 5, and because the inclusion of VHA/DoD hospitals in the OP_18b averages can pull a state's reported time toward the federal-system average. Any analysis that compares states should treat the four U.S. territories with extra care and disclose the federal-hospital inclusion when reporting absolute numbers.

raw_evidence.label: Scope guidance for the Analyst
raw_evidence.content: Recommendations: (a) Treat the 22 measure_ids as five logical groups — ED flow (OP_18b family, OP_22), Vaccination (HCP_COVID_19, IMM_3), Sepsis (SEP_1, SEP_SH_*), Stroke (STK_*), and Pregnancy/Behavioral (PC_01, SUB_, TOB_, IMM_2). (b) Compute state rankings ONLY for measures whose direction is consistent (lower-better OR higher-better — never mix). (c) Show OP-18b and HCP_COVID_19 head to head; their state-level distributions and outliers tell two completely different geographic stories. (d) For correlations, scatter ED time vs. healthcare worker COVID coverage by state — there is a non-obvious anti-correlation worth checking. (e) Keep the four territories visible but flagged separately so they don't distort state-level statistics. (f) For each measure, also report the count of reporting states so readers see when a measure is sparse.

sentences.summary: det_06: Sepsis (SEP_1) and stroke (STK) bundles. Source: Hospitals - Timely & effective care | CMS Provider Data Catalog (https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/topics/hospitals/timely-effective-care) Facts: SEP_1 is a composite measure of the early-management bundle for severe sepsis and septic shock; STK measures track antithrombotic, anticoagulation, and discharge therapy for ischemic stroke

raw_evidence.label: Sepsis (SEP_1) and stroke (STK) bundles
raw_evidence.content: Beyond the ED-flow and vaccination measures, the file carries condition-specific 'process bundles.' SEP_1 is a composite that asks whether a septic patient received the entire 3-hour and 6-hour bundle: lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluids for hypotension, repeat lactate, and vasopressors when indicated. National compliance hovers in the high-50s percent range and varies widely by state. STK measures (STK_2, STK_3, STK_5, STK_6) cover antithrombotic therapy, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, and antithrombotic at discharge for acute ischemic stroke patients — bundles where compliance is generally above 95%. The contrast — sepsis is hard to keep above 60% even today, stroke care has been pushed near ceiling — is itself one of the most teachable findings the data offers a general reader.
